A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NBF-based dialogue-safety framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original jailbreak-defense experiments, helpfulness evaluations, ablations, generalization tests and adaptive-attack results in Section 5 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds guardrail comparisons, over-refusal measurements, embedding experiments and further generalization tests.

M1.justification: The dialogue dynamics, four training losses and multi-turn filtering procedure remain unchanged. For the newly evaluated prompt-detection task, v2 adds an output adaptation declaring only predicted score 1 harmless (Appendix B.1); the retained dialogue-safety labeling treats scores 1–4 as safe.

E1.justification: v2 adds over-refusal evaluation on XSTest and benign JailbreakBench prompts, and prompt-harmfulness classification on HarmBench, AegisSafetyTest and WildGuardTest. Appendix B additionally evaluates consolidated single-turn attacks on SafeMT_ATTACK_600 and MHJ. These substantially broaden task and input-scenario coverage beyond v1's retained jailbreak and helpfulness evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 adds evaluated guardrail comparators OpenAI Moderation, ShieldGemma and LLaMAGuard. The original LoRA SFT and safe-system-prompt baselines remain; 'prompt-based steering' denotes the retained prompt baseline. X-Boundary is newly discussed but is not an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: v2 introduces F1 and over-refusal evaluation protocols, training that excludes ActorAttack and Opposite-day for held-out attack tests, and a DistilRoBERTa embedding configuration. The consolidated-attack evaluation specifies Acronym-based training and threshold 0.001. Previously stated training budgets, learning rates, temperature and principal attack procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Table 5 tests generalization after withholding two attack families from training. Table 6 adds embedding sensitivity and over-refusal outcomes to the loss ablations, while Table 9 examines robustness to attack consolidation. Existing threshold, non-invariant-turn, RedQueen, adaptive-attack and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental run counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. The existing assumption about consistency across LLM seeds is unchanged and does not report repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: Matched original safety, helpfulness and ablation values are retained, but v2 adds substantial result entries for refusal, guardrail detection, held-out attacks, embeddings and consolidated attacks. For example, new Table 4 reports HarmBench F1 values of 0.811 and 0.848 for the two NBF variants versus 0.672 for LLaMAGuard; these comparisons were absent from v1.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, assumptions, Equations (1)–(33), invariant-safety theorem, corollary and Appendix A proofs retain their substance under renumbering. Section 4.2 corrects the verbal description of the probability difference without changing Equation (5).

C1.justification: The central control-theoretic framework and invariant-safety contribution remain intact. The abstract and contribution statements extend comparative claims to prompt-based steering and lightweight guardrails, and add over-refusal to the safety–helpfulness trade-off. The novelty claim is qualified to online filtering before prompts reach the LLM.

C2.justification: v2 adds an interpretation of DistilRoBERTa as inducing a more aggressive safety boundary and MPNet as offering greater trade-off flexibility. It also discusses lightweight guardrail applicability and suggests agent topic-control applications in Appendix C. The earlier limitations concerning generalization, labeled data, filtering costs and adaptive attacks remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the alternative embedding identifier and model sizes, the prompt-detection label mapping, and training/threshold details for the consolidated-attack test. It adds a project-website link. The code link already existed in v1, and the original architecture, optimizer, loss-weight and hardware disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds a focused discussion of concurrent X-Boundary, distinguishing its fine-tuning approach from a transferable context-aware guardrail. It also adds references for evaluated moderation systems, embeddings, benchmarks and attack consolidation. The established positioning around multi-turn jailbreaks and neural control certificates remains.

P1.justification: The main section sequence, appendix organization and much of the prose remain intact. v2 makes localized revisions to the abstract, introduction and experimental narrative, clarifies the predictor description, and changes author presentation and citation style. The document is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 changes the publication template and document-wide typography and float placement. It splits v1 Table 2 into safety and helpfulness tables, expands existing tables with refusal and embedding columns or rows, and adds Tables 4, 5 and 9. All ten figures retain their underlying graphics, with placement and caption changes.

improvement.justification: The added guardrail comparisons, explicit over-refusal measurements and generalization analyses make practical applicability and safety costs better supported than in v1. Reporting weaknesses limit the gain: Table 5 does not specify its steering threshold, and Tables 3 and 6 report inconsistent Llama-3 XSTest refusal rates, 0.087 and 0.104, for apparently the same configuration. Overall, the expanded scrutiny provides a useful but qualified improvement.
